images.text:
Kristi: Hi. Did you want to talk to me?
Adam: Yes. Kristi, how do you feel about your second week here?
Kristi: It's been great! I think I've learned a lot, and I've worked on a lot of different parts of the production. There's a steep learning curve, but the training I received was really effective. It's been a great experience so far.
Adam: I believe you've done a really great job, and I'm really happy with your work. Like I said before, you are an asset to this team.
Kristi: Thanks! I reckon that you have been really welcoming and helpful, and that's made it easy for me to learn the ropes and settle into my role.

Adam: That was a really tight deadline, and you made it. The copy editors you worked with said that you picked up our style really quickly. It's not easy to switch from one style to a new one and I recognize that you have made great strides in learning our style and becoming comfortable and confident using it. The style we use is not like any other.

Kristi: I suppose it has been a little difficult getting used to it, but the people I was working with were really helpful and patient, and they helped me with any doubts I had. Rob showed me how to use the style guide properly, so that I could quickly find any rules that I needed to check.
Adam: Good. I'm glad everyone is being so accommodating. The staff we work with is great and always ready to pitch in and share the work. I suppose that we've been really lucky with our hiring!
Kristi: Yeah, and I feel really lucky to be here.

Relative clauses: Omitting Relative Pronouns and Reference Words
It is common to omit relative pronouns in defining relative clauses.

Relative pronouns (that, which, who, where, etc.) identify the object that you want to refer to in a defining relative clause. It is possible, however, to leave these words out in conversation.

Compare these two sentences:

The excuse which he made was unconvincing.
The excuse he made was unconvincing.

You cannot omit the relative pronoun when it is the subject of the clause.

For example:
The people who were sitting at the front couldn't hear anything.

Take a look at some other examples from the text.
The copy editors you worked with said that you picked up our style really quickly.
The style we use is not like any other.
I think I've learned a lot, and I've worked on a lot of different parts of the production.
The people I was working with were really helpful and patient.
The staff we work with is great and always ready to pitch in and share the work.
The Present Perfect Tense with Report/Comment Verbs and Phrases
You can use the Present Perfect with verbs like reckon, believe and suppose when you want to comment or report on what has been done.

When you use the Present Perfect, you refer to things that happened in the past but have a connection to the present. This is useful when you talk about how things affect you and your current situation.

For example:
I believe you've done a really great job, and I'm really happy with your work.
I reckon that you have been really welcoming and helpful.
I suppose that we've been really lucky with our hiring!

You use the past participle of the main verb in the Present Perfect tense.
I reckon that you have been really welcoming and helpful.
I recognize that you have made great strides in learning our style.
I suppose it has been a little difficult getting used to it.
I suppose that we've been really lucky with our hiring!
